newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO say barriers to Hebron deal remain.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO say barriers to Hebron deal remain.

text.p: The PLO said on Tuesday an Israeli demand to delay by two years a promised troop pullback from West Bank areas was a key obstacle to a deal on handing over most of Hebron town to Palestinian self-rule.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross renewed his mediation efforts between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan said Israel and the PLO agreed on most points but were wrangling over peace moves to follow Hebron.

Bar-Illan confirmed Israel wanted to postpone to 1999 the last of three Israeli redeployments from occupied rural West Bank areas which under a 1995 interim peace deal were to be completed by September 1997.
"The last redeployment is a very, very contentious issue. Our interpretations are very far apart," he told Reuters.

Bar-Illan said Netanyahu proposed to U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross in a pre-dawn meeting that Israel complete further West Bank pullouts by the spring of 1999, when the sides are slated to complete "final status" peace negotiations.
"When the final status talks are set to end we will implement the last redeployment because we will then know in which areas there will be a Palestinian Authority," he said.
PLO officials quickly blasted the Israeli proposal as a violation of timetables set under the original peace deal signed with Israel's previous Labour-led government.

"This is an irresponsible proposal...the agreement specifically states that the last stage of further redeployments from the West Bank be completed by September 7, 1997," negotiator Hassan Asfour told Reuters.
"I wish that Mr. Netanyahu will stick to the agreement and will honour his commitments to implement the agreements as they were signed," chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters.
Ross held talks with Netanyahu in Jerusalem on Tuesday. The prime minister's office did not signal any breakthroughs.
"The mediator will continue his contacts on both sides in an effort to advance the Hebron agreement," Netanyahu's office said in a statement.
Asfour accused Ross, who was due to shuttle to Gaza for evening talks with Arafat, of bias towards Israel.
"Unfortunately Ross' duty is to help Netanyahu and not to help the peace process. This leads to the loss of the basis of the neutrality of the American role," he told Reuters.
Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdainah said the PLO was seeking detailed American guarantees Israel would implement interim peace deals to the letter.
"We will not sign an agreement without American guarantees," Abu Rdainah told Reuters. PLO officials said the United States was willing to supply only vaguely worded guarantees.

Officials said the sides also differed over a Palestinian presence at Hebron's Cave of the Patriarchs, a site holy to Moslems and Jews slated to remain under Israeli control. The shrine is known to Moslems as al-Ibrahimi mosque.
Bar-Illan said Netanyahu and Arafat could meet soon to try again to hammer out a deal. The two leaders had met secretly on Saturday night.
Israel's handover of most of Hebron has been delayed for 10 months over security concerns and violence. The volatile city is home to 400 Jewish settlers and 100,000 Palestinians.
In a reminder of the violence threatening Hebron, a shackled Israeli soldier on Tuesday re-enacted for Israeli police investigators his shooting attack on Arab shoppers last week.

"I wanted to kill as many Arabs as possible," Noam Friedman, 22, said in remarks broadcast on Israel Radio. Friedman, who wounded seven Arabs in the shooting spree before he was wrestled to the ground by other soldiers, said he shot up Hebron's vegetable market to sabotage the pending handover.
